title: Adulting 101 · Episode 3
chapters: Medicare and finding a GP you trust

units.t: Adulting 101. Episode three.
In this episode: Stay safe online, First aid basics: DRSABCD, Medicare and finding a GP you trust and myGov without the headache.
Part one. Stay safe online.
A few simple habits stop the vast majority of account takeovers, and most take only minutes to set up.
Why you're a target.
Many people think, 'Why would a hacker want my stuff?'
But most attacks are not personal.
Criminals use automated tools to try millions of stolen passwords, send millions of phishing messages and scan for unpatched devices.
Your email account alone can be used to reset passwords for your bank, shopping and social media.
Stolen identities are sold and used for fraud.
Australia has seen major data breaches, like Optus and Medibank in 2022, exposing millions of people's details.
You do not need to be important to be worth attacking.
You only need to be reachable.
Passwords that work.
Length beats complexity.
A passphrase of four or more random words, like 'purple-kettle-marathon-cactus', is easier to remember and much harder to crack than a short jumble like P@ssw0rd1.
The most important rule is never reuse passwords.
When one website is breached, attackers automatically try the same email and password on banks, email and shopping sites, a technique called credential stuffing.
Your email password matters most of all.
Nobody can remember 100 unique strong passwords.
A password manager generates a random one for each site, stores them securely and fills them in.
You only remember one strong master password.
Built into Apple and Google devices and browsers, managers also help against phishing, because they will not autofill on a fake website.
Second steps and phishing.
Two-factor authentication, 2FA or MFA, adds a second step when you log in, such as a code from an authenticator app, a text message code, a fingerprint or a security key.
Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get in without it.
Turn it on for email, banking, myGov, social media and shopping.
Authenticator apps are more secure than text messages.
Never share a code with anyone who asks for it.
Phishing messages pretend to come from organisations you trust.
Warning signs include urgency or threats, generic greetings, odd sender addresses, spelling mistakes and mismatched links, but modern phishing can look flawless.
The safest habit: do not click links in unexpected messages.
Open the official app or type the address yourself.
Update and back up.
Software updates often patch security holes that attackers already know about and actively exploit.
The Australian Signals Directorate lists patching applications and operating systems among its most important cyber security strategies.
Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser and apps.
Very old phones and routers that no longer receive updates are a risk worth replacing.
Ransomware and device failure can wipe out photos and documents.
Back up important files regularly, ideally automatically to the cloud and to an external drive.
Lock your devices with a PIN, password or biometrics, and turn on 'find my device'.
Public Wi-Fi is less risky now that most websites are encrypted, but avoid banking on unknown networks.
Share less.
Scammers and identity thieves piece together information from social media: your birthday, hometown, school, pet's name and holiday dates.
These are often the answers to security questions, or useful for impersonation.
Review your privacy settings and limit what is public.
Think before posting in real time that you are away from home.
Be sceptical of quizzes asking for personal details.
If an organisation you use suffers a data breach, change that password and watch for follow-up scams.
The key idea: Most attacks are automated and impersonal, so every account has value to criminals.
Part two. First aid basics: DRSABCD.
The seven steps that could help you save a life.
An overview to build confidence, not a replacement for a proper course.
Learn the plan.
Knowing what to do in the first few minutes of an emergency can save a life.
When someone's heart stops, every minute without CPR sharply reduces their chance of survival, and ambulances can take several minutes or more to arrive.
Australian first aid follows an action plan called DRSABCD, from the Australian Resuscitation Council.
This lesson is an overview only.
A hands-on course, from organisations such as St John Ambulance or Australian Red Cross, is the best way to learn and practise.
D is Danger.
Before rushing in, check for danger to yourself, bystanders and the injured person: traffic, fire, electricity, deep water or aggressive people.
You cannot help anyone if you become a casualty yourself.
Wear gloves if available.
Response, then help.
R is Response.
Speak loudly and firmly squeeze their shoulders: can you hear me, open your eyes, what's your name, squeeze my hand.
If they respond, make them comfortable, check for injuries and monitor them.
If there is no response, get help.
S is Send for help.
Call Triple Zero, 000, or ask a bystander to while you help.
From a mobile, 112 also works.
Ask for an ambulance and put the phone on speaker.
The operator can guide you step by step, including through CPR, so you are not alone.
If an AED, defibrillator, is nearby, send someone to get it immediately.
Many are listed on apps and found at shopping centres, gyms and sporting clubs.
Airway and breathing.
A is Airway.
Look in the person's mouth for anything blocking it, such as vomit, blood, food or loose teeth.
If there is something, roll them onto their side and clear it.
Then, with the person on their back, gently tilt the head back and lift the chin.
For babies, keep the head in a neutral position rather than tilting it.
B is Breathing.
Look for the chest rising and falling, listen and feel for breath on your cheek, for up to 10 seconds.
Occasional gasping is not normal breathing and can happen in the first minutes after cardiac arrest.
If they are breathing normally, place them in the recovery position, on their side with the top leg bent, and watch them until help arrives.
If not, start CPR.
CPR buys time.
C is CPR, short for cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
It combines chest compressions with rescue breaths to keep some oxygen-carrying blood flowing to the brain and heart.
CPR on its own rarely restarts a stopped heart, but it buys precious time until a defibrillator or paramedics arrive.
Start as soon as you have found that the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
Starting quickly matters more than perfect technique.
The CPR lesson walks you through exactly how to do it, including rescue breaths and how to adjust for children and babies.
Using an AED.
The final D is Defibrillation: an electric shock that can reset a heart whose rhythm has become chaotic.
An automated external defibrillator, or AED, is built for untrained bystanders.
It analyses the heart rhythm itself and tells you what to do at every step.
Attach it the moment it arrives, keeping CPR going while it is set up.
Notice where AEDs are kept at your workplace, gym, sports club or local shops.
They are usually marked by a green sign with a heart and lightning bolt.
The CPR lesson covers using one step by step.
The key idea: Australian first aid follows DRSABCD, starting with checking for danger before you approach anyone.
Part three. Medicare and finding a GP you trust.
Most Australians carry a green card in their wallet without really knowing what it does.
Here is how Medicare works in practice, and how to find a doctor who will know you by name.
What Medicare covers.
Picture two people seeing the same GP on the same morning.
One walks out paying nothing, the other pays at the desk and gets part of it back a day later.
Both are using Medicare, Australia's public health scheme.
It pays a rebate, based on a government-set fee, for a long list of out-of-hospital services such as GP visits, many specialist consultations, blood tests and scans.
It also covers treatment as a public patient in a public hospital at no cost.
It does not cover most dental care, glasses, ambulance trips in most states or private hospital accommodation.
This is general information; details are at servicesaustralia.
gov.
au.
Cards, apps and bulk billing.
Citizens and permanent residents can enrol, as can some visitors from countries with reciprocal agreements.
Most Australians start on a parent's card, and you can apply for your own from age 15.
Linking Medicare to myGov lets you see claims, update bank details so rebates land in your account, and download a digital card.
If a clinic charges upfront, the rebate is often paid back within minutes.
When a GP bulk bills, they accept the rebate as full payment and you pay nothing.
Otherwise you pay the gap between their fee and the rebate.
Gaps vary widely, and some practices bulk bill only certain groups, such as children or concession card holders.
So ask first: 'Do you bulk bill, and if not, what will I be out of pocket for a standard consult?'
The safety net.
Some years are expensive.
A run of specialist visits, scans and tests can add up quickly, especially for out-of-hospital care.
The Medicare Safety Net is designed for this.
Once your gap payments for eligible services pass a threshold in a calendar year, Medicare pays a higher rebate for the rest of that year.
Individuals are registered automatically, but couples and families need to register together so their costs are combined, and many people forget.
You can do this through your Medicare online account in myGov.
Thresholds change each year, so check current figures on the Services Australia website rather than relying on an old number you heard from a friend.
A GP who knows you.
A GP who has seen you for years remembers that your blood pressure crept up last winter and that your father had heart trouble.
That continuity is linked with better management of long-term conditions and fewer unnecessary tests.
MyMedicare is a voluntary scheme where you register with one practice, which can unlock longer telehealth consultations.
Even without registering, stick with one clinic and, where possible, one doctor, and ask for a longer appointment when you have several issues.
To find a good one, try the healthdirect Service Finder, which lists nearby practices, hours and bulk billing, and ask friends what they like.
Notice whether the GP listens without rushing and explains things plainly.
If the fit is wrong, move on; your old practice can transfer your records.
After hours and emergencies.
Illness rarely keeps business hours.
The healthdirect helpline on 1800 022 222 connects you with a registered nurse, who can help you decide whether to see a GP, go to an urgent care clinic or head to hospital.

Many areas now have Medicare Urgent Care Clinics, which treat urgent but not life-threatening problems, such as minor fractures or cuts needing stitches, often without an appointment and without a fee.
Telehealth GP services can handle many simple issues by phone or video.
For chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke or serious injury, call triple zero, 000, straight away.
Save these options in your phone now so you are not searching in a panic later.
The key idea: Medicare pays a rebate for many out-of-hospital services and covers public patients in public hospitals at no cost.
Part four. myGov without the headache.
One login for Centrelink, Medicare, the tax office and more sounds simple, until you are stuck on hold.
Here is how to make the system work for you.
One front door.
Imagine you have just moved house.
Once, you might have filled in separate forms for the tax office, Medicare and Centrelink.
With myGov, you sign in once at my.
gov.
au and update your details for several services together.
myGov is not a service itself, more like a front door with a set of keys.
Behind it sit linked services such as the Australian Taxation Office, Medicare, Centrelink, Child Support, My Health Record and the Department of Veterans' Affairs, along with some state services.
You choose which ones to link.
Each service still holds its own records.
Linking just lets you reach them all from one place and receive their letters in one inbox.
Setting up and linking.
Type my.
gov.
au yourself and create an account with an email address only you can access, not a shared family email or a work address you might lose.
Choose a sign-in method such as a text code, an authenticator app, a passkey or the myID app; stronger options make break-ins harder.
Each adult should have their own account, even couples who share everything else.
Linking is where many people get stuck.
The ATO may ask for details from a past tax return, Medicare for your card number and recent claim, and Centrelink can give you a linking code if you call or visit.
These checks stop impostors.
Gather a payslip, tax file number, Medicare card, ID such as a licence or passport, and agency letters, then do it in one sitting at a desk.
Inbox and scams.
Many linked services now send letters to your myGov inbox instead of the post, including notices about payments, debts and tax, some with deadlines.
Missing one can be costly: if Centrelink asks you to confirm your income and you do not reply, your payment can be paused.
Turn on notifications, read letters in full and save important ones as PDFs.
Scammers also copy myGov.
A text may say you are owed a refund or your account is suspended, with a link to a fake site that steals your login.
Services Australia has said myGov texts and emails will not contain links asking you to sign in.
Close the message and type my.
gov.
au yourself, or use the official app.
If you entered details on a fake page, change your password and contact Services Australia.
Report scams to Scamwatch, scamwatch.
gov.
au.
Getting through to a person.
Most routine tasks, such as updating an address, reporting income or claiming a Medicare rebate, can be done online or in the app, often faster than waiting on the phone.
When you do need a person, prepare before you dial.
Have your customer reference number, your myGov sign-in, and a short note of what you need and what has happened so far.
Calls are usually quieter early in the morning and later in the week, though this varies.
Write down the date, the name or identifier of the person you spoke to and what they said.
Service centres can help in person, and Services Australia also offers interpreter services and support for people who are not comfortable online.
When things go wrong.
Government decisions are not always right.
If Centrelink cuts a payment or raises a debt you think is wrong, first ask for an explanation of how the decision was made.
You can then request a formal review, where someone not involved in the original decision looks again.
Time limits can apply, especially if you want any back pay, so act quickly.
Beyond that, independent bodies such as the Administrative Review Tribunal can review many decisions, and the Commonwealth Ombudsman investigates complaints about how agencies have treated you.
Free legal help is available through community legal centres and Economic Justice Australia's network.
This is general information; check the details for your situation on servicesaustralia.
gov.
au.
The key idea: myGov is one secure login that reaches many federal services, each of which still holds its own records.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why are ordinary people targeted by hackers?
Answer. Attacks are automated and email opens many accounts.
Question two. What should you do first, before approaching an injured person?
Answer. Check for danger to everyone nearby.
Question three. Which is covered by Medicare for most people?
Answer. Public patient care in a public hospital.
Question four. What is myGov?
Answer. One login reaching services that keep their own records.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
